The Northern whiting (Sillago sihama) is a commercially important sillaginid species distributed across the Indo-West Pacific region, where it inhabits shallow sandy coastal waters and estuarine environments. Early life stages of this teleost are particularly sensitive to thermal conditions, with embryonated eggs and yolk-sac larvae developing optimally under warm coastal temperatures. Experimental rearing studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] have documented that eclosion occurs after approximately 4.5 days [ab = approximately 4.5 days], a developmental pace consistent with other tropical sillaginids that produce small, pelagic eggs. The newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days following chorion rupture. At the moment of eclosion, these yolk-sac larvae possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00015 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00015 grams], a minimal initial mass that reflects the modest egg diameter of 0.66 mm reported for this species. This reduced hatchling size imposes a brief window for the onset of exogenous feeding before the point of no return is reached.

As the growing juvenile progresses through the post-settlement phase, somatic growth proceeds rapidly under favourable conditions, driven by high ingestion rates and efficient food conversion. Field surveys and laboratory growth studies indicate that Sillago sihama attains a maximum asymptotic size represented by an ultimate fork length of 31 centimeters [Li = 31 centimeters], a value that aligns closely with the upper size range reported for this species across its geographic distribution. Corresponding to this terminal length, the ultimate wet weight of fully grown adults averages approximately 215.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 215.6 grams], a body mass that reflects the slender, elongate body plan typical of benthic-foraging sillaginids. The length-weight relationship for this species follows an allometric exponent slightly above 3.0, indicating that mass increases somewhat faster than the cube of length as individuals approach their asymptotic dimensions. This species undergoes a gradual shift in habitat use as it matures, with smaller juveniles concentrating in very shallow protected embayments before dispersing into deeper coastal waters.

Reproductive development in the Northern whiting follows a seasonal pattern governed by water temperature and photoperiod, with gonadal recrudescence typically initiating during the warmer months. Puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and the first detectable vitellogenesis in females, is reached at a fork length at puberty of 16.7 centimeters [Lp = 16.7 centimeters]. This size at maturation corresponds roughly to the second year of life for most individuals in wild populations, though some variation exists across latitudinal gradients. The attainment of sexual maturity at this moderate body length allows females to channel significant energy reserves into gamete production without excessive delay, a life-history strategy common among iteroparous tropical fishes that experience relatively high natural mortality rates during their early years. Histological examination of ovarian tissue has confirmed that oocyte development proceeds synchronously within batches, supporting a multiple-batch spawning strategy over an extended breeding season that can last several months.

The reproductive output of Sillago sihama is considerable, reflecting its high fecundity and the energetic demands of producing numerous small pelagic eggs. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' core spawning season at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], individual females release approximately 166,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 166,000 eggs per spawning event] and are capable of spawning at a frequency of about one spawning event per year [F_R_i = about one spawning event per year] during peak reproductive periods. This extraordinarily high daily reproductive rate is among the highest documented for sillaginid fishes and is consistent with the species' relatively short lifespan and high natural mortality. The production of such large numbers of small, transparent eggs represents a classic r-selected life-history tactic, wherein parental investment per offspring is minimal and survival to adulthood depends on the sheer numerical abundance of larvae entering the planktonic environment.

Longevity estimates for the Northern whiting, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith increment analysis, indicate that the maximum lifespan for this species in tropical Australian waters reaches approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] when individuals experience the stable thermal regime of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This relatively compressed lifespan for a fish with an ultimate fork length of 31 centimeters [Li = 31 centimeters] reflects the high metabolic demands and accelerated growth rates characteristic of warm-water tropical species. Senescence becomes apparent after the fourth year, with a progressive decline in condition factor and reproductive output observed in older individuals. Comparative analysis with congeneric species from higher latitudes reveals that this lifespan is notably shorter than that of temperate sillaginids, which may live beyond 12 years, underscoring the profound influence of environmental temperature on life-history pace. The combination of early maturation and abbreviated longevity defines the demographic strategy of Sillago sihama as a fast-lived, high-turnover species well adapted to the variable and productive coastal ecosystems it inhabits.
